lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first letter declares love for Elizabeth's poetry and for her herself.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's reply thanking him with deep gratitude for his sympathy.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's promise that spring will bring them together.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: Elizabeth's delight in Robert's 'Flight of the Duchess,' showing her growing admiration.

lines.text: How must I feel, and what can, or could I say even if you let me say all?
lines.note: Robert's expression of gratitude and happiness in Elizabeth's friendship.

lines.text: When I had read that letter last night I did think so.
lines.note: Elizabeth's emotional response to Robert's declaration of love.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's declaration that his whole life is wound around Elizabeth.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert's promise to live and die with Elizabeth's ring and hair.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: Robert's wish that they live and die together in love.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's callback to Robert's chestnut tree from his first letter.

lines.text: But I will believe in the end now and henceforth—I will believe you are my very own Ba,—my best dream’s realization, my life’s fulfilment and consummation—and having discovered you, I shall live and die with you.
lines.note: Robert's resolve to live and die with Elizabeth as his dream realized.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's final letter before their elopement, declaring Robert her only love.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration of love, written in the earliest days of their correspondence.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth's wonder that Robert could regret missing the chance to meet her, showing how quickly their bond formed.

lines.text: I think before writing--or just after writing--such a sentence--but reflection only justifies my first feeling; I would rather go without your letters, without seeing you at all, if that advantaged you--my dear, first and last friend; my friend!
lines.note: Robert declares he would rather lose her letters entirely than allow them to cost her strength, a measure of his devotion.

lines.text: And who paints, and dares exhibit, E.B.B.'s self?
lines.note: Robert asks for a sketch of Elizabeth, a private request tied to her sonnets and a moment of growing intimacy.

lines.text: And now listen to me in turn.
lines.note: Elizabeth begins her reply after Robert's words have touched her more profoundly than she thought possible.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writes on the eve of a visit, unable to stop thinking of him even when they are about to meet.

lines.text: And now I will dare ... yes, dearest, kiss you back to my heart again; my own.
lines.note: Robert's tender reply, kissing her back to his heart, from the height of their declared love.

lines.text: Landor says 'come up higher and let us sit and eat together.'
lines.note: Robert quotes Landor's invitation to sit and eat together, a shared literary touchstone between them.

lines.text: Do you remember the purple lock of a king on which hung the fate of a city?
lines.note: Elizabeth's gift of a lock of hair, comparing it to a king's lock on which hung a city's fate.

lines.text: Now—dear, dearest Ba—let me begin the only way!—And so you are kissed whether you feel it or not—through the distance, what matter?
lines.note: Robert kisses Elizabeth through the distance on the morning after their secret marriage is set in motion.

lines.text: I would not say to you yesterday, perhaps could not, that you wrote ever so much foolishness to me in the morning, dearest, and that I knew it ever so well.
lines.note: Elizabeth reflects that she would not tell Robert he wrote foolishness, a mark of their deepening trust.

lines.text: Dearest, all dearest beyond my heart’s uttering, will you forgive me for that foolish letter, and the warmth, and—FOR ALL,—more than ever I thought to have needed to ask forgiveness for!
lines.note: Robert begs forgiveness for a foolish letter, showing how even their quarrels end in renewed devotion.

lines.text: Both of them approved of the French route, and urged me to go to them in Paris—‘And,’ said my uncle kindly, ‘when once we have you, we shall not bear to part with you, I think.’
lines.note: Elizabeth insists that no one around her must hear of Robert, guarding their secret to the last.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's final letter before their elopement, looking forward to having him alone at last.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first declaration of love, the seed from which everything in this correspondence grows.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first reply of gratitude, the door opening in return.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's promise that spring will bring their first meeting, the early moment of hope.

lines.text: I must thank you by one word for all your kindness and consideration--which could not be greater; nor more felt by me.
lines.note: Elizabeth thanking him after their first visit, marking the turn from letters to presence.

lines.text: I have but one greater delight in the world than in hearing from you.
lines.note: Robert naming hearing from her as his greatest delight besides, the attachment deepening.

lines.text: And then the next thing to write off my mind is ... that you must not, you must not, make an unjust opinion out of what I said to-day.
lines.note: Elizabeth's vulnerable confession of her brother's death, a private revelation only he receives.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writing on the eve of a visit, the rhythm of their meetings established.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's rapturous letter of love, the courtship at its height.

lines.text: Miss Barrett--which is gone, the friendship, so gone!)
lines.note: Elizabeth's playful farewell to 'Miss Barrett' as a friend, the old identity dissolving.

lines.text: My dear Christmas gift of a letter!
lines.note: Robert's Christmas gift of a letter, the first holiday they share by correspondence.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's callback to Robert's chestnut tree from the very first letters, their private mythology.

lines.text: No, my own dearest, I did not see you sit in your chair, nor in mine, yesterday—did I write nothing about your walking with me by the garden wall, and on the hill, and looking down on London?
lines.note: Robert's tender reply correcting her, the intimate quarrel-and-reconciliation of long love.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth on the eve of elopement, the love that has carried her to this moment.

lines.text: The boxes are safely sent.
lines.note: Elizabeth's final line before their departure, the journey about to begin.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration of love, the seed of everything that follows.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first grateful answer, showing her warmth and wit from the start.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: He looks ahead to meeting her in spring, a promise that runs through their letters.

lines.text: I never shall forget these things, my dearest friend; nor remember them more coldly.
lines.note: She recalls their private revelations after hearing of her brother's loss.

lines.text: For, observe, you have not done ... yes, the 'Prometheus,' no doubt ... but with that exception have you written much lately, as much as last year when 'you wrote all your best things' you said, I think?
lines.note: He turns his thought to duty and what she means to his work.

lines.text: And once he held my hand, ... how I remember! and said that he 'loved me better than them all and that he would not leave me ... till I was well,' he said! how I remember that!
lines.note: She remembers her brother's promise, a deeply private grief she shared with Robert.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: He writes of being entirely wrapped around her, a turning point in their intimacy.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: She says she cannot guess what he is to her, showing the depth of her feeling.

lines.text: That you glorify and change and, in returning then, give me!
lines.note: He gives heart and life, not merely poetry, defining their bond.

lines.text: I will care for it no more, dearest--I am wedded to you now.
lines.note: He declares himself wedded to her, moving from friendship to commitment.

lines.text: It was so warm, so warm, the thermometer at 68 in this room, that I took it into my head to call it April instead of January, and put on a cloak and walked down-stairs into the drawing-room--walked, mind!
lines.note: She walks down-stairs for the first time in months, a small victory shared with him.

lines.text: All but--(that is, all was wrong but)--to be just ... the old, dear, so dear ending which makes my heart beat now as at first ... and so, pays for all!
lines.note: He returns to the old dear ending, anchoring their love.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert’s first declaration of love, setting the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Will you take back my gratitude for it?--agreeing, too, that of all the commerce done in the world, from Tyre to Carthage, the exchange of sympathy for gratitude is the most princely thing!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s graceful thanks for his letter and her wish for poet-to-poet sympathy.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Her wondering whether he truly regretted not meeting her, and her gentle self-deprecation.

lines.text: I am writing too much,--and notwithstanding that I am writing too much, I will write of one thing more.
lines.note: She says something is in her heart to say, an early hint of the depth to come.

lines.text: In one thing, however, you are wrong.
lines.note: She denies his suggestion that he gives her too little, insisting on his worth.

lines.text: At least it does not prevent my going on to agree with the saying of Spiridion, ... do you remember?...
lines.note: Their shared talk of inspiration and revelation, showing their intellectual bond.

lines.text: But I never did strike you or touch you--and you are not in earnest in the complaint you make--and this is really all I am going to say to-day.
lines.note: Her protest that she never struck him, with playful, intimate reassurance.

lines.text: They sent me down you know to Torquay--Dr. Chambers saying that I could not live a winter in London.
lines.note: She begins the painful story of her brother’s death, a turning point of trust.

lines.text: But we may be friends always ... and cannot be so separated, that your happiness, in the knowledge of it, will not increase mine.
lines.note: She says they may be friends always, and that his happiness increases hers.

lines.text: But now you have done with me until Tuesday.
lines.note: She tells him their time together need not end yet, holding the bond open.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert’s great avowal that his whole life is wound round and over her.

lines.text: Mr. Kenyon was here on Sunday and talking of the poems with real living tears in his eyes and on his cheeks.
lines.note: Mr. Kenyon moved to tears by Robert’s poems, a moment of public recognition.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: Robert’s wish that they live and die in love, under God’s will.

lines.text: Because if I am exacting it is for you and not for me--it is altogether for you--you understand that, dearest of all ... it is for you wholly.
lines.note: Elizabeth’s confession that her exactingness is wholly for his sake.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's opening declaration of love for her verses and for her, the very first word of the correspondence.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: The companion line that crowns the opening letter with its plain confession of love.

lines.text: And was the little book written with Mr. Mill, pure metaphysics, or what?
lines.note: Robert's tender wish that she will outlast the east wind, an early promise of care.

lines.text: Are you not my dear friend already, and shall I not use you?
lines.note: Elizabeth's reply turning their growing bond into friendship, the first mutual naming.

lines.text: And now, what will people say to this and this and this--or 'O seclum insipiens et inficetum!' or rather, O ungrateful right hand which does not thank you first!
lines.note: Elizabeth's grateful reading of his new book, where love of the giver exceeds the gift.

lines.text: There is nothing in you that does not draw out all of me.
lines.note: Robert's answer that she possesses him, the mirror of his earlier devotion.

lines.text: I read Luria's first act twice through before I slept last night, and feel just as a bullet might feel, not because of the lead of it but because shot into the air and suddenly arrested and suspended.
lines.note: Elizabeth reading Luria's first act, the bullet arrested in air, their creative partnership begun.

lines.text: What are you doing to me?--in the heart's heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's midnight joy at his late-arriving letter, the lovers' vigil.

lines.text: Ah, love,--you are my unutterable blessing,--I discover you, more of you, day by day,--hour by hour, I do think!--I am entirely yours,--one gratitude, all my soul becomes when I see you over me as now--God bless my dear, dearest.
lines.note: Robert's discovery of her, more of her, day by day, the deepening of love.

lines.text: And now, my Audience, my crown-bearer, my path-preparer--I am with you again and out of them all--there, here, in my arms, is my proved palpable success!
lines.note: Elizabeth's walk down-stairs, the feat of recovery that closes the winter of illness.

lines.text: At from half-past three to four, then—four will not, I suppose, be too late.
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letters in the carriage, the final journey begun.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's farewell of the letters she cannot leave behind, the love made portable.

lines.text: Do you pray for me to-night, Robert?
lines.note: Elizabeth's prayer for him on the last night, the voice of the final letter.

lines.text: I begin to think that none are so bold as the timid, when they are fairly roused.
lines.note: Elizabeth's closing word on Wilson's fidelity, the last line of the conversation.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first direct declaration of love to Elizabeth.

lines.text: You let 'flowers be sent you in a letter,' every one knows, and this hot day draws out our very first yellow rose.
lines.note: Robert sends roses in a letter, beginning their private language of flowers.

lines.text: I never shall forget these things, my dearest friend; nor remember them more coldly.
lines.note: Elizabeth says she will never forget what Robert has given her.

lines.text: It is something to me between dream and miracle, all of it--as if some dream of my earliest brightest dreaming-time had been lying through these dark years to steep in the sunshine, returning to me in a double light.
lines.note: Elizabeth describes Robert's love as a dream returned in double light.

lines.text: I would rather look at my seventy-five letters--there is room to breathe in them.
lines.note: Elizabeth counts their letters rather than the days they have known each other.

lines.text: What are you doing to me?--in the heart's heart.
lines.note: Robert asks what Elizabeth is doing to him in the heart's heart.

lines.text: Dear, dear heart of my heart, life of my life, will this last, let me begin to ask?
lines.note: Robert wonders whether this happiness can last and whether he can deserve it.

lines.text: It was simply to your thoughts, that I replied ... and that you need not say to yourself any more, as you did once to me when you brought me flowers, that you wished they were diamonds.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks Robert to stop wishing his flowers were diamonds.

lines.text: But where no eye can see; save your dear eye ... there is written a dedication.
lines.note: Robert writes a private dedication to Elizabeth inside a parcel.

lines.text: But I will believe in the end now and henceforth—I will believe you are my very own Ba,—my best dream’s realization, my life’s fulfilment and consummation—and having discovered you, I shall live and die with you.
lines.note: Robert promises to live and die with Elizabeth.

lines.text: It was so,—could not but be so—and I always loved you, as I shall always.
lines.note: Robert recalls that his first word to Elizabeth was 'I love you.'

lines.text: Dearest—dearest, you did once, one time only, call me by my name—Robert; and though it was to bid ‘R. not talk extravagances’ (your very words) still the name so spoken became what it never had been before to me.
lines.note: Robert remembers Elizabeth calling him by his name.

lines.text: Dearest, if you feel that, must I not feel it more deeply?
lines.note: Elizabeth says she feels Robert's letter more deeply than she thought.

lines.text: Dearest Ba, my very own, I love you with a love—not to die before any sorrow! perhaps that is the one remaining circumstance of power to heighten it!
lines.note: Robert calls their two years a glorious dream without blankness.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Early promise of friendship and spring meeting.

lines.text: See now, how, of that 'Friendship' you offer me (and here Juliet's word rises to my lips)--I feel sure once and for ever.
lines.note: Robert's certainty of their friendship.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's hope to see her in spring.

lines.text: You wished all manner of good to me one day as the clock struck ten; yes, and I assure you I was better that day--and I must not forget to tell you so though it is so long since.
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls his clock-striking kindness.

lines.text: Do you suppose that your power of giving and refusing ends when you have shut your room-door?
lines.note: Robert's quiet devotion before their first meeting.

lines.text: I read the poem many years ago, and never since, though I have an impression that the versification is good, yet from your commentary I see I must have said a good deal more in its praise than that.
lines.note: Robert on her music and creative process.

lines.text: As for going abroad, that is just the thing I most want to avoid (for a reason not so hard to guess, perhaps, as why my letter was slow in arriving).
lines.note: Robert's reluctance to go abroad (for her).

lines.text: 'I was to see you--and you were to understand'--Do you? do you understand--my own friend--with that superiority in years, too!
lines.note: Robert's tender appeal to be understood.

lines.text: But I never did strike you or touch you--and you are not in earnest in the complaint you make--and this is really all I am going to say to-day.
lines.note: Elizabeth's reassurance after his complaint.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's declaration of being wound around her.

lines.text: When I first saw you--I saw your eyes--since then, you, it should appear, see mine--but I only know yours are there, and have to use that memory as if one carried dried flowers about when fairly inside the garden-enclosure.
lines.note: Robert's memory of their first meeting.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert's joy in her ring and hair.

lines.text: You are the most entirely lovable creature I ever dreamed perhaps might be in a better world—altogether made up of affectionateness and generosity.
lines.note: Robert on her affectionateness.

lines.text: I begin to think that none are so bold as the timid, when they are fairly roused.
lines.note: Elizabeth's final farewell and trust in Wilson.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration of love, establishing the emotional starting point.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: A vivid promise of meeting in spring that carries their longing forward.

lines.text: I must thank you by one word for all your kindness and consideration--which could not be greater; nor more felt by me.
lines.note: Elizabeth's grateful reply after their first visit, showing trust beginning to deepen.

lines.text: I have but one greater delight in the world than in hearing from you.
lines.note: Robert's simple statement of how much her letters mean to him.

lines.text: And you are NOT, NOT my 'other friend,' any more than this head of mine is my other head, seeing that I have got a violin which has a head too!
lines.note: A playful, private rejection of being treated as merely another friend.

lines.text: God bless you for all you have been, and are, and will certainly be to me, come what He shall please!
lines.note: Elizabeth's overwhelmed gratitude and sense of the weight of his love.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's sweeping image of being wrapped entirely around her.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: A tender vow to live and die with her gift, marking their secret bond.

lines.text: Yet He knows,--if the entireness of a gift means anything,--that I have not given with a reserve, that I am yours in my life and soul, for this year and for other years.
lines.note: Elizabeth's quiet, total surrender of herself to him.

lines.text: But deep down, deeper than the Sirens go, deep underneath the tides, there, I bless and love you with the voice that makes no sound.
lines.note: A deeply private expression of love spoken without sound.

lines.text: It is my own especial fairy-tale ... from the spells of which, may you be unharmed...!
lines.note: Elizabeth frames their extraordinary connection as her own fairy-tale.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Echoes the earlier chestnut-tree image from one of Robert's first letters (s512).

lines.text: You are the whole world to me—and the stars besides!
lines.note: A final, expansive declaration that she is his whole world and the stars besides.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's closing image of having him only, to love her, as they prepare to leave.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's opening declaration of love for her verses and for her, the spark of everything that followed.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first reply, thanking him from the bottom of her heart and naming his sympathy the quintessence of sympathy.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's early promise that in spring he would surely see her, and that he never failed to get what he set his heart upon.

lines.text: I must thank you by one word for all your kindness and consideration--which could not be greater; nor more felt by me.
lines.note: Elizabeth thanking him for his kindness and consideration after their first visits had begun, when she was still learning to trust him.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: A private joke in their teasing register: Robert tied like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl, Elizabeth wielding the cudgel, a mock-horror they both recognise.

lines.text: But your 'Saul' is unobjectionable as far as I can see, my dear friend.
lines.note: Elizabeth on 'Saul', unobjectionable and holding her until it blesses her, an early sign of how his work moved her.

lines.text: I am unhappy enough even where I am happy--but ungrateful nowhere--and I thank you from my heart--profoundly from the depths of my heart ... which is nearly all I can do.
lines.note: Elizabeth unhappy even where she is happy, thanking him profoundly, one of the first tremors of what she could not yet say.

lines.text: Do not be angry with me--do not think it my fault--but I do not go to Italy ... it has ended as I feared.
lines.note: Elizabeth's decision not to go to Italy with her brother, the hard necessity that kept her in England and in his reach.

lines.text: All to-day, Friday, Miss Mitford has been here!
lines.note: Miss Mitford's five-hour visit and Elizabeth tired of talking, a glimpse of the world around their letters.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writing while about to see him, and her bullet-shot feeling on reading the first act of Luria.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's confession that his whole life is wound up and over her, the love she could not yet believe in.

lines.text: Thank you! and will you, if your sister made the copy of Landor's verses for me as well as for you, thank her from me for another kindness, ... not the second nor the third?
lines.note: Elizabeth thanking him for Landor's verses and the praise that came with them, the poetry that was always between them.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's farewell-tinged callback to his early chestnut-tree letter, proof that she remembered from the very beginning.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first declaration of love to Elizabeth.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth's gracious reply accepting the lost opportunity.

lines.text: Some things you say are very touching, and some, surprising; and although I am aware that you unconsciously exaggerate what I can be to you, yet it is delightful to be broad awake and think of you as my friend.
lines.note: Elizabeth's blessing on Robert's joy.

lines.text: I have all to say yet--next letter.
lines.note: Robert's brief promise of more to come.

lines.text: Before you come, try to forgive me for my 'infinite kindness' in the manner of consenting to see you.
lines.note: Elizabeth's gentle consent to see him.

lines.text: Pomegranates you may cut deep down the middle and see into, but not hearts,--so why should I try and speak?
lines.note: Robert's metaphor of hearts and pomegranates.

lines.text: And once he held my hand, ... how I remember! and said that he 'loved me better than them all and that he would not leave me ... till I was well,' he said! how I remember that!
lines.note: Elizabeth's painful memory of her brother.

lines.text: 'Tell me what I have a claim to hear': I can hear it, and be as grateful as I was before and am now--your friendship is my pride and happiness.
lines.note: Robert's avowal of love's onward prospect.

lines.text: And just so late last night, five letters were found in the letter-box, and mine ... yours ... among them--which accounts for my beginning to answer it only now.
lines.note: Elizabeth's joy at receiving his letters.

lines.text: And ungrateful, too; with the real sufficing happiness here of being, and knowing that you know me to be, and suffer me to tell you I am yours, ever your own.
lines.note: Robert's vow to live and die with her gifts.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's whole life wound around her.

lines.text: See what is here, since you will not let me have only you to look at--this is Landor's first opinion--expressed to Forster--see the date! and last of all, see me and know me, beloved!
lines.note: Robert's note of Landor's praise.

lines.text: Yes--'yours' it must be, but you, it had better be!
lines.note: Elizabeth's tender word for their bond.

lines.text: My dear Christmas gift of a letter!
lines.note: Robert's Christmas gift of a letter.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's very first letter: love for her verses and for her.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: The first avowal of love, setting everything in motion.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's early promise to see her come spring.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: Elizabeth's praise of the Duchess, early shared work.

lines.text: On the subject of your letter--quite irrespective of the injunction in it--I would not have dared speak; now, at least.
lines.note: Robert grateful for her admission to her inner feelings.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writing even though they meet tomorrow.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's whole life wound round her.

lines.text: It comes at eight o'clock--the post says eight ...
lines.note: Elizabeth counting the post's arrival, daily devotion.

lines.text: Can I speak?
lines.note: Elizabeth overwhelmed that he has done everything for her.

lines.text: It was so,—could not but be so—and I always loved you, as I shall always.
lines.note: Robert loving the affectionateness and generosity in her.

lines.text: Oh, how can you, blessing me so, speak as you spoke yesterday—for the first time!
lines.note: Robert hurt that she spoke as she did the day before.

lines.text: I should not have said those words, certainly I should not—but you forgive them and me, do you not?
lines.note: Elizabeth's retraction and forgiveness offered.

lines.text: You asked me yesterday ‘if I should repent?’
lines.note: Robert wishing the past could be done over for her.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letter before they marry and leave.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's very first letter to Elizabeth, declaring love for her verses and for her — the beginning of everything.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first reply, thanking him from the bottom of her heart — the opening of the correspondence.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's spring letter anticipating their first meeting, asking 'when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?'

lines.text: Did I thank you with any effect in the lines I sent yesterday, dear Miss Barrett?
lines.note: Robert's post-meeting letter expressing thanks, marking the transition from letters to visits.

lines.text: Well--I have really been out; and am really alive after it--which is more surprising still--alive enough I mean, to write even so, to-night.
lines.note: Elizabeth reporting she has been out walking — a milestone in her recovery and a sign of growing trust.

lines.text: You are all that is good and kind: I am happy and thankful the beginning (and worst of it) is over and so well.
lines.note: Robert's warm response to Elizabeth's first outing, calling her 'all that is good and kind.'

lines.text: And Papa's answer was--burnt into me, as with fire, it is--that 'under such circumstances he did not refuse to suspend his purpose, but that he considered it to be very wrong in me to exact such a thing.'
lines.note: Elizabeth's painful confession about her brother's death — the deepest personal revelation she made to Robert.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writing before their next meeting, showing how the visits have become the centre of her life.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: Robert's refusal to imagine losing her — 'MORE; having a right to expect more strength with the strange emergency.'

lines.text: It is something to me between dream and miracle, all of it--as if some dream of my earliest brightest dreaming-time had been lying through these dark years to steep in the sunshine, returning to me in a double light.
lines.note: Elizabeth's 'between dream and miracle' — the moment she acknowledged the transformation Robert had wrought in her life.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's callback to Robert's early letter about the chestnut tree — showing how their words have woven into their shared memory.

lines.text: Yes, you are better, I think.
lines.note: Elizabeth's relief at Robert's recovery, marking the deepening of mutual care in the final months before their secret marriage.

lines.text: I go to you, my Ba, with heart full of love, so it seems,—yet I come away always with a greater capacity of holding love,—for there is more and still more,—that seems too!
lines.note: Robert's declaration that he goes to her 'with heart full of love' — the sustained intensity of his devotion.

lines.text: But dearest, dearest, ... when did I try to dissuade you from telling all to your father and mother?
lines.note: Elizabeth's defence of Robert against worldly suspicion — 'when did I try to dissuade you from telling all to your father and mother?'

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first direct avowal of love.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first heartfelt gratitude.

lines.text: See now, how, of that 'Friendship' you offer me (and here Juliet's word rises to my lips)--I feel sure once and for ever.
lines.note: Robert's early certainty of friendship.

lines.text: May God bless you, my dear friend.
lines.note: Elizabeth's blessing as she grows better.

lines.text: Next Wednesday--if you know how happy you make me! may I not say that, my dear friend, when I feel it from my soul?
lines.note: Robert's joy at a promised meeting.

lines.text: This I will say, then--wait and know me better, as you will one long day at the end.
lines.note: Robert's promise to be known better over time.

lines.text: I shall see you to-morrow and yet am writing what you will have to read perhaps.
lines.note: Elizabeth writes before seeing him again.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's whole life wound around her.

lines.text: How you overcome me as always you do--and where is the answer to anything except too deep down in the heart for even the pearl-divers?
lines.note: Elizabeth overcome by his tenderness.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls the chestnut tree.

lines.text: No, my own dearest, I did not see you sit in your chair, nor in mine, yesterday—did I write nothing about your walking with me by the garden wall, and on the hill, and looking down on London?
lines.note: Robert's playful denial about her chair.

lines.text: But, dearest of all, you never said a word about Monday.
lines.note: Elizabeth notes the missing Monday.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration of love to Elizabeth, setting the correspondence in motion.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's grateful, heartfelt reply, the beginning of their mutual regard.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's promise that spring will bring their first meeting, a recurring hope.

lines.text: As for going abroad, that is just the thing I most want to avoid (for a reason not so hard to guess, perhaps, as why my letter was slow in arriving).
lines.note: Robert's refusal to go abroad, because it would mean leaving Elizabeth, a turning point in commitment.

lines.text: Well--I have really been out; and am really alive after it--which is more surprising still--alive enough I mean, to write even so, to-night.
lines.note: Elizabeth's joy at having been out and alive after it, a small triumph of health.

lines.text: If you told me your love was bestowed elsewhere, and that it was in my power to serve you there, to serve you there would still be my pride and happiness.
lines.note: Robert's avowal that even her love bestowed elsewhere would be his pride and happiness.

lines.text: When I had read that letter last night I did think so.
lines.note: Elizabeth deeply touched by Robert's words, a moment of surrender.

lines.text: How good and kind to send me these books! (The letter I say nothing of, according to convention: if I wrote down 'best and kindest' ... oh, what poorest words!)
lines.note: Elizabeth's delight in Robert's gifts and kindness, her warmth throughout.

lines.text: But this shall do--I am not going to prove what may be, when here it is, to my everlasting happiness.
lines.note: Robert's vow to live and die with Elizabeth's ring and hair, tokens of their bond.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: Robert's prayer that they live and die so, sealing their lifelong union.

lines.text: Now—dear, dearest Ba—let me begin the only way!—And so you are kissed whether you feel it or not—through the distance, what matter?
lines.note: Robert's playful kiss across the distance, their affection undimmed.

lines.text: No. I care as little for money as you do—but this thing I will not agree to, because I ought not.
lines.note: Elizabeth's refusal to let Robert sacrifice his money for her sake.

lines.text: I will go for a licence to-day and we can be married on Saturday.
lines.note: Robert's decisive plan to marry at once before Elizabeth's departure.

lines.text: The boxes are safely sent.
lines.note: Elizabeth's final preparations, sending her letters and books ahead, ready to leave with Robert.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: R's opening declaration that he loves her verses with all his heart and loves her too — the first spark of their correspondence.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: R's early avowal that he loves her books and her — the seeds of their bond.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: E's first reply, thanking R from the bottom of her heart — showing she was deeply moved.

lines.text: I must thank you by one word for all your kindness and consideration--which could not be greater; nor more felt by me.
lines.note: E thanking R for kindness and consideration, showing how much she felt it — their growing closeness.

lines.text: Which reminds me that he knows of your having been here, of course! and will not mention it; as he understood from me that you would not.--Thank you!
lines.note: E noting Kenyon knows R has been here and will not mention it — the discretion of their secret meetings.

lines.text: Instead of writing this note to you yesterday, as should have been, I went down-stairs--or rather was carried--and am not the worse.
lines.note: E praising R's poem as too good for college prizes — their shared literary world.

lines.text: But have you not discovered by this time that I go on talking with my thoughts away?
lines.note: R admitting he talks with his thoughts away — his self-deprecating charm.

lines.text: I read Luria's first act twice through before I slept last night, and feel just as a bullet might feel, not because of the lead of it but because shot into the air and suddenly arrested and suspended.
lines.note: E comparing reading Luria's first act to a bullet suspended in air — their creative collaboration.

lines.text: It ('Luria') is all life, and we know (that is, the reader knows) that there must be results here and here.
lines.note: E saying Luria is all life — praise of his work.

lines.text: When you write will you say exactly how you are? and will you write?
lines.note: E asking R to say exactly how he is — tender concern for his health.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: R saying he loves her more if she never writes again — devotion beyond words.

lines.text: No, my own dearest, I did not see you sit in your chair, nor in mine, yesterday—did I write nothing about your walking with me by the garden wall, and on the hill, and looking down on London?
lines.note: R denying he saw her sit in her chair but recalling their walk by the garden wall — their secret visits.

lines.text: Your letters to me I take with me, let the ‘ounces’ cry out aloud, ever so.
lines.note: E saying his letters are with her — keeping his words close.

lines.text: I tried to leave them, and I could not.
lines.note: E saying she tried to leave but could not — her inability to part from him.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration of love to Elizabeth, setting the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: I do not find it take away from my feeling of the magnanimity of Prometheus that he should, in truth, complain (as he does from beginning to end) of what he finds himself suffering.
lines.note: Robert's reading of Prometheus shows the shared literary ground and seriousness with which he meets her.

lines.text: God bless you.
lines.note: Robert's promise of verse and of being seen, early in the friendship.

lines.text: May God bless you, and let you hold me by the hand till the end--Yes, dearest friend!
lines.note: Robert asking to be held by the hand, the tenderness that defines their bond.

lines.text: I write one word just to say that it is all over with Pisa; which was a probable evil when I wrote last, and which I foresaw from the beginning--being a prophetess, you know.
lines.note: Elizabeth's announcement that Pisa is lost, a turning point in their story.

lines.text: Love me, my own love; not as I love you--not for--but I cannot write that.
lines.note: Robert's first unguarded 'love me' after the declared attachment.

lines.text: I read Luria's first act twice through before I slept last night, and feel just as a bullet might feel, not because of the lead of it but because shot into the air and suddenly arrested and suspended.
lines.note: Elizabeth's bullet metaphor on reading his Luria, a vivid private image.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert's gratitude for the ring and hair, tokens of their private covenant.

lines.text: My dear Christmas gift of a letter!
lines.note: Robert's Christmas letter, the love declared as his truest song.

lines.text: 'I shall love thee to eternity'--I shall.
lines.note: Elizabeth's sortes oracle, 'I shall love thee to eternity.'

lines.text: No, my own dearest, I did not see you sit in your chair, nor in mine, yesterday—did I write nothing about your walking with me by the garden wall, and on the hill, and looking down on London?
lines.note: Robert's gentle correction that he did not see her sitting, early after the marriage resolve.

lines.text: Still—remember my ‘peculiarity’—with the greater I keep the less, you let me say and praise me for saying—so, with all the dear hope of to-morrow,—now, my Ba—and now, I kiss you.
lines.note: Robert's 'peculiarity' kept alongside the greater love, a signature tenderness.

lines.text: Robert! because, my Robert, if gravely I distrusted your affection, I could not use such light-sounding words on the whole—now could I?
lines.note: Elizabeth finally speaking his name, 'Robert,' a long-awaited intimacy.

lines.text: At from half-past three to four, then—four will not, I suppose, be too late.
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letter, sending off the boxes and counting the hours to departure.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush’s ecstatic reunion shows how much the dog’s love mirrors Elizabeth’s own.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert admits he sometimes shortened visits just to reach the moment of taking Elizabeth’s hand.

lines.text: Bless you, Ba.
lines.note: A tender sign-off that closes one of their early, anxious letters.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s cry over losing Flush captures the sudden panic of that day.

lines.text: I shall go through it, as certainly as that I love you.
lines.note: She promises to endure whatever comes because her love for Robert is certain.

lines.text: Poor Flush—how sorry I am for you, my Ba!
lines.note: Robert’s sympathy for Flush’s plight shows his care for Elizabeth’s whole world.

lines.text: Remember Flush—to write.
lines.note: A small, caring reminder that keeps Flush’s rescue thread alive.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush’s return, sprawled on the sofa, gives Elizabeth a rare moment of relief.

lines.text: No, dearest, I am not to see you to-morrow for all the happiness of the permission!
lines.note: Robert has to cancel a longed-for visit because his health will not allow it.

lines.text: Take care of yourself, dearest dearest, and if you think of me and love me, show it in that best way.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks Robert to prove his love by resting and taking care of himself.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: After the secret wedding, Elizabeth is relieved that the dangerous day is over.

lines.text: All that I am, I owe you—if I enjoy anything now and henceforth, it is through you.
lines.note: Elizabeth credits Robert with lifting her from despair into life and sunshine.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Robert’s gratitude for her secret note seals the depth of his devotion.

lines.text: Your letters to me I take with me, let the ‘ounces’ cry out aloud, ever so.
lines.note: Elizabeth insists on carrying Robert’s letters with her despite the ounces.

lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Early reassurance that she understood him from the start.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush's ecstatic reunion shows her world and tenderness.

lines.text: If I did not love you, how I would begin now!
lines.note: His love declared as something that would begin now if it had not already.

lines.text: I have just come from the vestry of Paddington chapel, and bore it very well, and saw nobody except one woman.
lines.note: She faces the church crowd and manages her nerves.

lines.text: ‘Comfort me with apples, for I am sick of love!’
lines.note: His apple parable about not delaying what matters.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Flush is stolen, turning their private worry into action.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: She binds the Flush ordeal to their own bond: she is his Flush.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush recovered and resting after the ransom ordeal.

lines.text: And smiling to myself I was, both last night and this morning, at your phrase about the ‘business’ to be talked by the ‘grave man and woman’; understanding your precaution against all unlawful jesting!—jesters forbidden in the protocol!
lines.note: She smiles at his grave-man-and-woman business talk.

lines.text: We must be married directly and go to Italy.
lines.note: He presses for immediate marriage as delay becomes dangerous.

lines.text: I did hate so, to have to take off the ring!
lines.note: She hates removing the ring and wants it restored.

lines.text: You take my words from me—I ‘exult’ in the irrevocability of this precious bestowal of yourself on me—come what will my life has borne flower and fruit—it is a glorious, successful, felicitous life, I thank God and you.
lines.note: He exults in the irrevocable gift of herself.

lines.text: Oh—if I loved you less ... a little, little less.
lines.note: Final letter: she would tell him if she loved him less.

lines.text: You overcome me with goodness—there’s the real truth, and the whole of it.
lines.note: Early tenderness: Elizabeth says Robert's goodness overwhelms her.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Private shared life: Flush's ecstatic welcome shows Elizabeth's home world.

lines.text: Every day shows me more to love in you, dearest, and I open my arms as wide as I can ...
lines.note: Robert's growing love frames the courtship's emotional turn.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Crisis over Flush becomes a recurring callback between them.

lines.text: And now that you probably have him by your side, I will tell you what I should have done in such a case, because it explains our two ways of seeing and meeting oppression lesser or greater.
lines.note: Robert's Flush advice reveals their contrasting temperaments.

lines.text: My own Ba, if I thought you could fear me, I think I should have the courage to give you up to-morrow!
lines.note: Robert refuses to rule Elizabeth by fear, a key promise.

lines.text: Was ever any in the world, in any possible world, so perfectly good and dear to another as you are to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth answers his goodness with unmatched devotion.

lines.text: We must be married directly and go to Italy.
lines.note: Urgency turns courtship into decisive action.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: Elizabeth commits her will entirely to Robert.

lines.text: Words can never tell you, however,—form them, transform them anyway,—how perfectly dear you are to me—perfectly dear to my heart and soul.
lines.note: Robert tries to express love beyond words before the wedding.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: Elizabeth reports the wedding day survived and safe.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Robert's gratitude answers Elizabeth's wedding-day note.

lines.text: Bless you, my very own, only Ba—my pride, and joy, and utter comfort.
lines.note: Robert's family accepts Elizabeth, deepening the bond.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Final letter marks the end of their secret correspondence.

lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Opens with her insistence that she already understood your words, setting the early intimacy.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush's ecstatic reunion shows how fiercely she feared losing him before Italy.

lines.text: Let them call it ‘felony’ or ‘burglary’—so long as they don’t go to church with us, and propose my health after breakfast!
lines.note: Your joke reframes their elopement as adventure rather than scandal.

lines.text: ‘Comfort me with apples, for I am sick of love!’
lines.note: The apple counsel playfully warns against waiting too long.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Flush's sudden loss becomes a shared crisis and test of her resolve.

lines.text: Do not let our happiness be caught up from us, after poor Flush’s fashion—there may be no redemption from that peril.
lines.note: You warn against letting their happiness be caught up like Flush.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush is found and lying on the sofa after the ransom drama.

lines.text: No, dearest, I am not to see you to-morrow for all the happiness of the permission!
lines.note: You are kept from seeing her by illness just when permission seemed granted.

lines.text: Do you think your wishes, much less your blessings, fall to the ground, my own Ba?
lines.note: Your question about wishes falling to ground answers her anxious letters.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: After the wedding, she reports all is safe so far.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Your gratitude acknowledges the proof of love she risked.

lines.text: First, God is to be thanked for this great joy of hearing that you are better, my ever dearest—it is a joy that floats over all the other emotions.
lines.note: She thanks God for your recovery amid the work ahead.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Her final letter looks toward having only each other by the next day.

lines.text: The happier Tuesday, if on Tuesday comes the writer of the letters!
lines.note: Elizabeth names the happy Tuesday when Robert's letters arrive, an early rhythm of longing.

lines.text: How I miss you, and long for Friday.
lines.note: She says plainly how she misses him and longs for Friday, the feeling the poem is for.

lines.text: I am your very own, dearest dearest, with you or away from you.
lines.note: Robert answers that he is hers with or away from her, a steady early promise.

lines.text: I thought once that the capacity of happiness was destroyed in me, but you have made it over again,—God has permitted you!
lines.note: Elizabeth says Robert made her capacity for happiness over again.

lines.text: I have just come from the vestry of Paddington chapel, and bore it very well, and saw nobody except one woman.
lines.note: She reports getting through the vestry, a small victory in their cautious waiting.

lines.text: ‘Comfort me with apples, for I am sick of love!’
lines.note: Robert's apple counsel turns worry about timing into their private shared language.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Elizabeth's cry that she has lost Flush shows the domestic crisis they weather together.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: She turns the Flush dispute into the tender line that she is his Flush and he is hers.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush is found again on the sofa, bringing relief after the danger.

lines.text: What a glorious dream; through nearly two years—without a single interval of blankness,—much less, bitter waking!
lines.note: Robert remembers their dream lasting nearly two years without a blank interval.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: Elizabeth gives one will that is his as the plan becomes real.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: She writes that all is safe after the overwhelming wedding day.

lines.text: I did hate so, to have to take off the ring!
lines.note: She hates taking off the ring and asks him to put it on again.

lines.text: You take my words from me—I ‘exult’ in the irrevocability of this precious bestowal of yourself on me—come what will my life has borne flower and fruit—it is a glorious, successful, felicitous life, I thank God and you.

lines.note: Her final letter, asking if this is the last, closes the farewell.
